claims.text: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy is as-cast with a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure.
The alloy should be solutionized at approximately 900°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere.
Solutionizing at 900°C for 1 hour will homogenize and prepare the microstructure.
A subsequent aging treatment at about 500°C for 8 hours will precipitate coherent nanoscale B2-ordered phases.
Rapid quenching after aging is part of the proposed treatment.
An inert processing atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
Precise temperature control during the two treatment stages will preserve the fine lamellar architecture and produce uniform nanoprecipitates.
The treatment will form nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates uniformly along the lamellar boundaries.
Coherent B2 precipitates will act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The B2 precipitates will pin the lamellar interfaces.
Obstruction of dislocation motion and interface pinning will restrict creep deformation.
Precipitation hardening will increase yield strength.
Interface pinning will stabilize the microstructure during thermal cycling and long-term mechanical loading.
The precipitation treatment will delay grain-boundary sliding.
Maintaining a stable microstructure will improve corrosion resistance in corrosive environments.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the as-cast alloy.
The treated alloy will exhibit less room-temperature creep than the as-cast alloy.
The treated alloy will have improved fatigue resistance under combined extreme conditions.
The treatment will maintain adequate ductility relative to the as-cast state.
The treatment will maintain adequate corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast state.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifically claims lower room-temperature creep, but the proposed creep experiment is conducted at an elevated temperature such as 500°C; that test cannot directly falsify the room-temperature creep claim.

The falsification rule describes failure using a creep-strain reduction of greater than 20%, even though such a reduction would normally represent successful improvement. The intended failure threshold appears to be a reduction below 20%, making the stated rule ambiguous.
